newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian, Ukrainian leaders hail political pact.
newsitem.headline: Romanian, Ukrainian leaders hail political pact.

text.p: The presidents of Romania and Ukraine put decades of mistrust behind them on Monday by signing a long-delayed treaty that could boost Romania's chances of fast-track NATO admission.

Romania's Emil Constantinescu and his Ukrainian counterpart Leonid Kuchma signed a treaty aimed at settling differences over borders, left over from a pact signed some 60 years ago between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union.
"I declare in all solemnity that we are together experiencing a historic moment," Constantinescu said after the signing in the Black Sea resort of Neptun.

The treaty, three years in the making, will dampen arguments related to land lost by Romania under the 1939 Soviet-Nazi pact, but differences remain over borders in the Black Sea which both sides believe to be rich in oil and gas.
"Now the key word is trust and the signing should be followed by concrete action," Constantinescu told reporters.
Under the 1939 pact, Moscow annexed Romania's lands of Bucovina, southern Bessarabia and Serpent Island, now in Ukraine.

The treaty signed on Monday proclaims the borders between the two former communist states as "inviolable". It also deals with the issue of Romanian and Ukrainian ethnic minorities in the two countries.

By settling its borders issue with Ukraine -- seen as a last hurdle for Bucharest's NATO bid -- Romania has switched into high gear in its race towards membership of the Western alliance, Constantinescu said.
"Romania fulfils now all conditions to be accepted in the first wave. Absolutely all conditions," he said.
NATO is expected to invite Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary to join its ranks at a summit in Madrid next month. Romania and Slovenia are also pushing hard to join.
Kuchma also hailed the treaty as historic and said it would lay the ground for a new era between the two neighbours.
"There were always suspicions between us. This treaty will help us forget the past, in the name of the future," he said.
Kuchma was greeted with military honours when he arrived at the signing ceremony, which took place at the former summer residence of late Stalinist dictator Nicolae Ceaucescu.

Constantinescu said he was confident Romania's parliament, where his centrist forces have a comfortable majority, would ratify the treaty "very fast" despite opposition by leftist parties to the document.

Leaders of the leftist opposition refused to attend the signing ceremony, which was timed with an eye to the NATO summit. Several NATO members have expressed their backing for Romania, but key members Germany and the United States have yet to offer explicit support.
